name: Head and Neck Cancer
aliases: head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

clinicalPearls: Most head and neck cancers are squamous cell carcinomas arising from the mucosal surfaces of the paranasal sinuses, oral cavity, nasopharynx, oropharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx (Harrison 22e p.610).
Alcohol and tobacco are the most significant environmental risk factors and act synergistically when used together; smokeless tobacco is an etiologic agent for oral cancers (Harrison 22e p.610).

In Western countries, HPV (predominantly HPV-16) causes over 50% of oropharyngeal cancers (tonsillar bed and base of tongue); these occur in younger patients and carry a better prognosis, especially in nonsmokers (Harrison 22e p.610-611).

EBV infection is frequently associated with nasopharyngeal cancer, especially in endemic areas (East Asia, some Mediterranean countries); EBV antibody titers can be used to screen high-risk populations (Harrison 22e p.610).

HPV testing should be performed at diagnosis for all patients with oropharyngeal tumors; HPV-related disease has a more favorable AJCC 8th-edition staging (advanced nodal stage can still be equivalent to overall early stage) (Harrison 22e p.611-613).

Panendoscopy under anesthesia (laryngoscopy, esophagoscopy, bronchoscopy) with multiple directed biopsies is the definitive staging procedure to establish diagnosis, define extent, and identify second primaries (Harrison 22e p.611).

When a head and neck lesion treated initially with antibiotics does not resolve in a short period, further workup is indicated; simply continuing antibiotics may lose the chance for early diagnosis of a malignancy (Harrison 22e p.611).

For an enlarged cervical node with no visible primary, diagnose by fine-needle aspiration or lymph node excision; if squamous cell carcinoma, perform panendoscopy with directed biopsies of nasopharynx, tonsil, tongue base, and pyriform sinus (Harrison 22e p.611-612).

Most parotid tumors are benign, but about half of submandibular and sublingual tumors and most minor salivary gland tumors are malignant; adenoid cystic carcinoma tends to recur along nerve tracks and metastasize as late as 10-20 years (Harrison 22e p.610-611, 613).
harrison.pathophysiology: Squamous cell carcinomas arise from the mucosal surfaces of the upper aerodigestive tract. The entire pharyngeal mucosa is exposed to alcohol- and tobacco-related carcinogens, producing field cancerization with risk of premalignant lesions (erythroplakia, leukoplakia) progressing through hyperplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma in situ to invasive carcinoma. In HPV-negative tumors, p53 mutations are frequent along with mitotic-signaling and Notch pathway alterations and dysregulated cell-cycle control. HPV oncogenes drive carcinogenesis by directly inhibiting the p53 and RB tumor-suppressor genes; HPV-positive tumors carry a distinct mutational signature with frequent PI3K pathway alteration. EGFR is frequently overexpressed and correlates with poor prognosis. EBV is associated with undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma (lymphoepithelioma) (Harrison 22e p.610-611).
additionalDifferentials: Carcinoma of unknown primary presenting as cervical adenopathy without an identifiable mucosal lesion
Salivary gland tumors (mucoepidermoid, adenoid cystic carcinoma, adenocarcinoma)
Sarcoma, including radiation therapy-induced sarcoma after prior radiotherapy
Metastasis to supraclavicular nodes from a primary site in the chest or abdomen
nonInfectiousMimics: Premalignant mucosal lesions (leukoplakia, erythroplakia) representing hyperplasia, dysplasia, or carcinoma in situ
additionalInvestigations: Thorough otolaryngologic examination including inspection of all visible mucosal surfaces and palpation of the floor of mouth, tongue, and neck
CT or MRI of the head and neck to define disease extent (comparably accurate, 65-90%, for cervical nodal metastases)
CT of chest and upper abdomen for patients with lymph node involvement to screen for distant metastases; chest CT also screens for second lung primary in heavy smokers
PET scan to identify or exclude distant metastases and assess treatment response
Endoscopic examination under anesthesia (panendoscopy) with multiple biopsies
Fine-needle aspiration or excisional lymph node biopsy when no primary is visible
HPV testing of oropharyngeal tumors at diagnosis; EBV antibody titers / plasma EBV DNA for nasopharyngeal cancer screening
TNM staging per AJCC (varies by anatomic subsite)
redFlags: Persistent hoarseness requiring referral for indirect laryngoscopy and/or radiographic studies (possible early laryngeal cancer)
Non-healing ulcer of the oral cavity
Persistent neck mass / cervical lymphadenopathy, especially a solitary, hard, nontender node in an older chronic tobacco user
Dysphagia, odynophagia, or decreased tongue mobility
Sore throat and/or otalgia, or a head/neck lesion that does not resolve after antibiotics
Unilateral serous otitis media, nasal obstruction, or epistaxis (nasopharyngeal cancer); cranial neuropathies from skull base involvement
Head and neck symptoms persisting longer than 2-4 weeks
harrison.prognosis: Poorly differentiated tumors have a worse prognosis than well-differentiated tumors. Overt distant metastases are present in <10% at diagnosis. HPV-related oropharyngeal cancers consistently carry a better prognosis (reflected in a separate, more favorable AJCC 8th-edition staging system), especially in nonsmokers. For localized disease (about one-third of patients), overall 5-year survival is 60-90%, with most recurrences occurring within the first 2 years and usually local. For locally/regionally advanced disease (>50% of patients at presentation), 5-year survival exceeds 50% in many trials (partly due to the increasing fraction of HPV-related tumors); advanced nasopharyngeal cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by concomitant chemoradiotherapy has achieved 5-year survival exceeding 80% in a Southeast Asian study. Patients cured of early-stage tobacco/alcohol-related disease are at greater risk of dying from a second malignancy than from recurrence of the primary (Harrison 22e p.611-613).
pitfalls: Continuing antibiotic treatment for a non-resolving head and neck lesion rather than pursuing workup may delay diagnosis of malignancy (Harrison 22e p.611).

Fine-needle aspiration should not be the first diagnostic procedure for a suspicious cervical node when a head and neck primary is suspected; perform a careful ENT exam and biopsy any suspicious mucosal lesion first (Harrison 22e p.4012-type cross-reference, p.611).

EGFR overexpression does not reliably predict response to EGFR inhibitors (active in only ~10-15% as single agents); substituting cetuximab for cisplatin in HPV-related cancers has shown inferior survival (Harrison 22e p.611, 613).
Retinoid supplements (e.g., cis-retinoic acid) have not been shown to prevent head and neck (or lung) cancer and may increase risk in active smokers (Harrison 22e p.610).
About 50% of patients develop hypothyroidism after treatment; thyroid function should be monitored (Harrison 22e p.613).
harrison.severityClassification: Clinically categorized into three groups: (1) localized disease (T1-T2 / stage I-II without nodal or distant spread), (2) locally or regionally advanced disease (large primary and/or cervical nodal metastases, lymph-node positive), and (3) recurrent and/or metastatic disease below the neck. Staged by the AJCC TNM system, which varies by anatomic subsite: primary tumors T1-T3 by increasing size with T4 representing invasion of adjacent structures (bone, muscle, root of tongue), and nodes staged by size, number, and laterality. A separate, more favorable staging system applies to HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer in the AJCC 8th edition (Harrison 22e p.611-613).
management: Deliver stage- and site-directed multimodality treatment combining surgical resection, radiotherapy, and concurrent platinum-based chemoradiotherapy according to tumour extent
Use targeted and immune therapy in advanced disease, with the epidermal-growth-factor-receptor inhibitor cetuximab and immune checkpoint inhibitors for recurrent or metastatic tumours
Perform HPV testing at diagnosis to refine staging and prognosis and to inform enrolment in de-escalation protocols for HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer
Provide supportive care with nutritional and feeding support, pre-radiotherapy dental assessment, speech and swallowing therapy, and alcohol and tobacco cessation
Manage treatment toxicities such as mucositis and xerostomia
Undertake structured surveillance for locoregional recurrence and second primary tumours with clinical examination and imaging
Coordinate care through a head and neck multidisciplinary team spanning surgery, oncology, radiotherapy, dietetics, and speech therapy, with early palliative care for advanced disease
